ideas.name: Effect sizes shrink on replication because original estimates are winner's-curse inflated
ideas.statement: A published effect size is typically an overestimate of the true effect because only studies that happened to produce large enough estimates to reach significance get published or noticed, so replications with the same true effect will tend to find smaller numbers.
ideas.whyYouNeedIt: Without this, the repeated finding across many replication projects that 'effect sizes shrink by half' would look like a mysterious coincidence rather than the predictable result of selection on significance.

occurrences.quote: 36% replicated successfully (p value below 0.05), with effect sizes averaging half the original magnitude
occurrences.reasoning: reports the shrinkage pattern as if self-explanatory, relying on reader to supply the selection mechanism

occurrences.quote: the replicated effect sizes were only 66% of the original reported effect sizes on average, suggesting that the original studies' effect sizes were inflated
occurrences.reasoning: names inflation but assumes reader knows why selection causes it

occurrences.quote: Underpowered[clarification needed] studies have a large effect size bias.
occurrences.reasoning: asserts the link between low power and inflated effect size without spelling out the selection mechanism

ideas.name: Publication bias as a selective filter, not a lie
ideas.statement: Journals and researchers preferentially publish positive, significant results and bury null ones, so the visible literature is a biased sample of all studies actually conducted, even when no individual study is fraudulent.
ideas.whyYouNeedIt: Without this idea, claims that 'most published findings are false' or that a 'file drawer' of invisible negative results exists would seem to require individual dishonesty rather than following from an aggregate selection process.

occurrences.quote: Publication bias—the tendency to publish only positive, significant results—creates the "file drawer effect", where negative results remain unpublished.
occurrences.reasoning: depends on readers already grasping selection-filter logic to see why a biased literature results

occurrences.quote: it is plausible that a considerable proportion of research findings might be false positives
occurrences.reasoning: the leap from bias existing to false positives dominating needs the selection-filter framing

occurrences.quote: Suppose the null hypothesis is true; how many publications would be required to make the current result indistinguishable from the null hypothesis?
occurrences.reasoning: the fail-safe number concept presupposes unpublished null results exist unseen

ideas.name: Incentive structures, not individual dishonesty, systematically select for unreliable science
ideas.statement: When career rewards (publications, grants, citations) attach to producing novel, positive, surprising results rather than true ones, the overall population of research practices will drift toward unreliability over time even if every individual scientist behaves in a locally reasonable way.
ideas.whyYouNeedIt: This is needed to make sense of claims that 'publish or perish' culture and citation advantages for irreproducible papers are structural problems requiring systemic reform, rather than just a matter of catching bad actors.

occurrences.quote: the goals and values of single scientists (e.g., publishability) are not aligned with the general goals of science (e.g., pursuing scientific truth)
occurrences.reasoning: relies on an evolutionary/structural view of incentives shaping the whole field's output

occurrences.quote: Under certain parameter settings, the population of labs converge to maximum productivity even at the price of very high false positive rates
occurrences.reasoning: models cultural evolution of practice as selection on incentives rather than individual choice

occurrences.quote: papers in leading general interest, psychology and economics journals with findings that could not be replicated tend to be cited more over time
occurrences.reasoning: shows citation incentives rewarding exactly the unreliable work, assuming reader connects this to systemic drift

ideas.name: Reproducibility of analysis and replicability of findings are distinct properties
ideas.statement: Being able to rerun the same analysis on the same data and get the same numbers is a different, weaker guarantee than a new, independent study finding the same result, and a field can have one without the other.

occurrences.quote: Reproducibility in a narrow sense refers to reexamining and validating the analysis of a set of data. The second category, replication, involves repeating an experiment or study with new, independent data
occurrences.reasoning: draws the distinction explicitly

occurrences.quote: Reproducibility can also be distinguished from replication, as referring to reproducing the same results using the same data set
occurrences.reasoning: reinforces the distinction with a definition

occurrences.quote: Open data, open source software and open source hardware all are critical to enabling reproducibility in the sense of validation of the original data analysis
occurrences.reasoning: shows reforms targeting the narrower reproducibility property specifically

ideas.name: Researcher degrees of freedom inflate false positives without fraud
ideas.statement: Because any study involves many small, defensible choices in design and analysis, researchers can unconsciously pick the combination that yields significance, raising the true false-positive rate far above the nominal 5% even with no intent to deceive.

occurrences.quote: Questionable research practices are behaviors that exploit researcher degrees of freedom (researcher DF)—choices in study design, data analysis, or reporting—to inflate false positive rates
occurrences.reasoning: directly states the concept

occurrences.quote: These choices in the "garden of forking paths" multiply, creating many "researcher degrees of freedom"
occurrences.reasoning: extends the idea to the full pipeline of choices

occurrences.quote: moderately flexible data analysis, routine in research, can increase the false-positive rate to above 60%
occurrences.reasoning: gives the quantitative consequence of the idea

ideas.name: Low power makes replication unlikely even for true effects
ideas.statement: The chance that a repeat study will again find a significant result depends mathematically on the statistical power of the original test, and when that power is as low as 20-35% (as in much of psychology and neuroscience), most true effects will fail to replicate purely by the math, regardless of fraud or error.

occurrences.quote: the probability of replicating a previous publication that rejected a null hypothesis in favor of an alternative is assuming significance is less than power
occurrences.reasoning: states the mathematical dependency of replication probability on power

occurrences.quote: on average, psychology studies have between 33.1% and 36.4% statistical power
occurrences.reasoning: gives the empirical power estimate that drives the predicted replication failure rate

occurrences.quote: estimating a median statistical power of 21%
occurrences.reasoning: applies the same low-power logic to neuroscience

ideas.name: Heterogeneity means there may be no single 'true effect size' to replicate
ideas.statement: When an effect genuinely varies across populations, settings, or hidden moderating conditions, repeated studies can disagree with each other not because of error but because they are correctly measuring different true values in different contexts.

occurrences.quote: Heterogeneity (variance in research findings due to multiple true effect sizes rather than one)
occurrences.reasoning: states the concept directly

occurrences.quote: this suggested that heterogeneity could have been a genuine characteristic of the phenomena being investigated
occurrences.reasoning: applies it to explain disagreement among direct replications

occurrences.quote: replication success is not likely even if replications have very large sample sizes
occurrences.reasoning: draws out the consequence that sample size cannot fix heterogeneity-driven disagreement

ideas.name: Bayesian updating, not the p-value, tells you how likely a finding is true
ideas.statement: The probability that an effect is real after a significant result depends on the prior probability it was true before the study, combined with the test's power and significance level—not on the p-value alone—so the same 'p < 0.05' can mean very different things depending on context.

occurrences.quote: rejecting the null hypothesis at significance level 5% does not mean that the posterior probability for the alternative hypothesis is 95%
occurrences.reasoning: states the core confusion being corrected

occurrences.quote: conditional on the statistical studying finding to be true, the posterior probability of actually being true is not
occurrences.reasoning: develops the formal Bayesian correction

ideas.name: A rejected null hypothesis does not confirm any specific alternative
ideas.statement: Finding that data is unlikely under 'no effect' only rules out that one hypothesis; it does not by itself support any particular substantive explanation, especially in fields where many competing theories would all predict the same rejection.

occurrences.quote: evidence against the null hypothesis "there is no correlation" is no evidence for one of the many alternative hypotheses that equally well predict "there is a correlation"
occurrences.reasoning: states the core logical gap

occurrences.quote: it does not imply the alternative hypothesis "ESP exists"
occurrences.reasoning: applies the idea to a concrete case

occurrences.quote: a theory makes a directional prediction and is tested by checking whether the null hypothesis is rejected in the right direction
occurrences.reasoning: contrasts soft-science use of this weak inference with physics

ideas.name: Most tested hypotheses being false a priori can explain low replication without misconduct
ideas.statement: If only a small fraction of hypotheses entering a field's testing pipeline are actually true, then even a well-run statistical process with standard error rates will generate a literature dominated by false positives, independent of any bad practice.

occurrences.quote: a possible reason for the low rates of replicability in certain scientific fields is that a majority of tested hypotheses are false a priori
occurrences.reasoning: states the mechanism

occurrences.quote: the claim that a majority of tested hypotheses are false a priori in certain scientific fields might be plausible given factors such as the complexity of the phenomena
occurrences.reasoning: ties the mechanism to field-specific plausibility
